notes.front: What is a power of attorney (POA) in dealings with the IRS?
notes.back: A taxpayer's written authorisation for an individual to receive their confidential tax information and act for them before the IRS.
notes.explanation: Publication 947 describes it as written authority given to an individual; Form 2848 is the IRS form that grants it.
notes.example: Like a signed letter letting your accountant speak for you at the bank, but limited to the tax matters and years it names.
notes.source: Publication 947 (Rev. February 2018), Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney, “What Is a Power of Attorney?”, p. 7

notes.front: What is a recognized representative?
notes.back: An individual recognised to represent a taxpayer before the IRS, appointed on Form 2848 or another acceptable power of attorney.
notes.explanation: Form 2848 is the IRS form for appointing one, and the representative completes its Part II declaration.
notes.example: Like the named agent on a letting agreement: once appointed, the agent deals with the other side for the owner.
notes.source: Publication 947 (Rev. February 2018), Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney, “Form Required”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Use IRS Form 2848 to appoint a recognized

notes.front: What is a closing agreement?
notes.back: A written agreement with the IRS that finally determines a tax matter, such as Form 906, Closing Agreement on Final Determination Covering Specific Matters.
notes.explanation: Form 906 is one closing agreement form the IRS Manual names among the documents that close issues settled in Appeals.
notes.example: Like a signed full-and-final settlement between two businesses, but with the IRS on the other side of a tax issue.
notes.source: IRM 4.10.7, Issue Resolution, “IRM 4.10.7.5.6.5.2, SB/SE FTS Closing Package”
notes.evidence: Form 906, Closing Agreement on Final Determination Covering Specific Matters

notes.front: What is a durable power of attorney?
notes.back: A power of attorney with no time limit that stays in force after the taxpayer becomes incapacitated or incompetent.
notes.explanation: The glossary of Publication 947 defines it by its survival past the principal’s incapacity or incompetency.
notes.example: Like a standing instruction to a relative that still works if you are later too ill to give instructions yourself.
notes.source: Publication 947 (Rev. February 2018), Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney, “Glossary: Durable power of attorney”, p. 16

notes.front: What is a tax information authorization (TIA)?
notes.back: A taxpayer's consent, usually on Form 8821, letting a named designee inspect or receive their confidential tax information.
notes.explanation: Form 8821 can name any individual, corporation, firm, organisation or partnership as the designee.
notes.example: Like giving your mortgage broker read-only access to your bank statements: they can look, but cannot act for you.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8821 (Rev. September 2021), Tax Information Authorization, “Purpose of Form”, p. 1

notes.front: What is the Centralized Authorization File (CAF)?
notes.back: The IRS computer file that records who is authorised under powers of attorney and tax information authorizations.
notes.explanation: Because the file holds the authority on record, IRS staff can check a representative without asking for the original document.
notes.example: Like a building’s visitor list at reception: staff check the list rather than asking each visitor for their letter of invitation.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2848 (Rev. September 2021), Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, “Line 4. Specific Use Not Recorded on the CAF”, p. 5

notes.front: In IRS practice, what is a fiduciary?
notes.back: A trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian who stands in the taxpayer's position and acts as the taxpayer.
notes.explanation: Form 56 is the form that tells the IRS a fiduciary relationship exists.
notes.example: Like the executor of a late relative’s will, who signs the final tax return in the relative’s place.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2848 (Rev. September 2021), Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, “Form 56”, p. 1

notes.front: What is the Transcript Delivery System (TDS)?
notes.back: An online IRS application that lets eligible practitioners view a client's return and account information in a secure session.
notes.explanation: It is reached with login credentials and is aimed at practitioners acting for clients.
notes.example: Like a bank’s adviser portal where an authorised adviser pulls a client’s statements online instead of asking the client to post copies.
notes.source: Transcript Delivery System (TDS), IRS.gov, “Transcript Delivery System (TDS)”
notes.evidence: Use TDS to view your client's return and account information quickly, in a secure, online session.

notes.front: What is a collection information statement?
notes.back: A financial statement (Form 433-F, 433-A or 433-B) the IRS may ask for to judge a taxpayer's ability to pay.
notes.explanation: The IRS uses the financial information on it to decide whether a taxpayer qualifies for relief such as a delay in collection.
notes.example: Like the income and outgoings form a lender asks you to fill in before agreeing to reschedule a loan.
notes.source: Temporarily delay the collection process, IRS.gov, “Required information”
notes.evidence: Form 433-A, Collection Information Statement for Wage Earners and Self-Employed Individuals

notes.front: What are the IRS Collection Financial Standards?
notes.back: Allowances for living expenses the IRS uses to help determine a taxpayer's ability to pay a delinquent tax liability.
notes.explanation: They set the amounts the IRS will accept for items such as food, housing and transport when it analyses a taxpayer’s finances.
notes.example: Like a debt adviser’s budget guide that caps what counts as a reasonable grocery bill for a family of four.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “General”
notes.evidence: Collection financial standards are used to help determine a taxpayer's ability to pay a delinquent tax liability.

notes.front: In a bankruptcy case, what is the automatic stay?

notes.explanation: It binds all entities, including the IRS as a governmental unit, from the petition date.
notes.example: Like a referee’s whistle that stops play for everyone the moment the petition is filed.
notes.source: Publication 908 (12-2025), Bankruptcy Tax Guide, “The automatic stay”, p. 15

notes.back: Write the word revoke, in capitals, across the top of the first page, sign and date it below, and send a copy to the IRS.
notes.explanation: The annotated copy goes by mail or fax to the address in the Where To File Chart or the office handling a specific matter.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2848 (Rev. September 2021), Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, “Revocation of a power of attorney”, p. 3
notes.evidence: a new representative, you must write “REVOKE” across the top

notes.front: How does a representative withdraw from representation?
notes.back: Write “WITHDRAW” across the top of the first page of the power of attorney, sign and date it, and send a copy to the IRS.
notes.explanation: It is the same process as a taxpayer’s revocation, done by the representative.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2848 (Rev. September 2021), Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, “Withdrawal by representative”, p. 3

notes.back: Write “WITHDRAW” across the top of the first page, sign and date it, and send a copy to the IRS.
notes.explanation: That is the withdrawal procedure in the Form 2848 instructions.

A) Write “WITHDRAW” on the first page, sign, date and send a copy
B) Write the word revoke on it
C) Just stop answering the IRS

notes.back: When the representative unreasonably delays the matter by not providing non-privileged information after repeated requests.
notes.explanation: Such conduct can also be referred to the Office of Professional Responsibility.
notes.source: Publication 947 (Rev. February 2018), Practice Before the IRS and Power of Attorney, “Dealing With the Representative”, p. 12

notes.front: What is Form 56 used for?
notes.back: To notify the IRS that a fiduciary relationship exists.
notes.explanation: A fiduciary acts as the taxpayer, so the IRS needs notice of who is acting.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2848 (Rev. September 2021), Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, “Form 56”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Relationship, to notify the IRS of the existence of a fiduciary

notes.front: Who signs a power of attorney appointing a representative for a person or entity that has a fiduciary?
notes.back: The fiduciary, on behalf of the person or entity.
notes.explanation: The fiduciary stands in the position of the person or entity.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2848 (Rev. September 2021), Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, “Form 56”, p. 1
notes.evidence: the person or entity, the fiduciary must sign the power of attorney

notes.front: After her father dies, Maria is appointed executor and wants to deal with his final return herself. Is she his representative under a power of attorney?
notes.back: No. As executor she is a fiduciary who acts as the taxpayer; she notifies the IRS on Form 56.
notes.explanation: A fiduciary stands in the taxpayer’s position, not as a representative.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, she needs Form 2848
B) No, she acts as the taxpayer and files Form 56
C) No, she needs Form 8821
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: she is not a representative. C is wrong: Form 8821 only allows information to be shared.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2848 (Rev. September 2021), Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, “Form 56”, p. 1

notes.front: Must the attorney of record in a case docketed in the Tax Court file a power of attorney with the IRS?
notes.back: No. The Tax Court has its own rules of practice, so the attorney of record needs none.
notes.explanation: Anyone other than the attorney of record who deals with the IRS on the docketed case does need one.
notes.source: Publication 216 (Rev. 3-92), Conference and Practice Requirements (26 CFR 601, Subpart E), “§601.509, Power of attorney not required in cases docketed in the Tax Court”, p. 10
notes.evidence: attorney is not required to be submitted by an attorney of

notes.front: What is the general rule of section 6103 for returns and return information?
notes.back: They are confidential and may be disclosed only as the Internal Revenue Code authorises.
notes.explanation: Section 6103 then lists the officers and others who may not disclose them.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6103, Confidentiality and disclosure of returns and return information, “§6103(a), General rule”
notes.evidence: Returns and return information shall be confidential

notes.front: What does section 6103(c) do to a person who receives return information under a taxpayer’s consent?
notes.back: Limits their use and disclosure of it and makes them liable to penalties for unauthorised access, use or redisclosure.
notes.explanation: Penalties can be brought by private right of action.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8821 (Rev. September 2021), Tax Information Authorization, “What’s New: Taxpayer notification”, p. 1
notes.evidence: consent and holds the recipient subject to penalties,

notes.front: May an e-file provider pass a return’s information to another provider to prepare and transmit it, without the taxpayer’s consent?
notes.back: Yes. Disclosure among providers for preparing the return is permissible without consent.
notes.explanation: Any other disclosure or use without consent can bring the section 7216 and 6713 penalties.
notes.source: Publication 1345 (Rev. 12-2025), Handbook for Authorized IRS e-file Providers of Individual Income Tax Returns, “Disclosure of Tax Return Information”, p. 36
notes.evidence: preparing a tax return is permissible without the taxpayer’s consent.

notes.front: A preparer wants to send a client’s return information to a lender for a refund-related loan the client has asked about. What must the preparer secure first?
notes.back: The taxpayer’s written consent that meets the section 7216 regulations.
notes.explanation: Publication 1345 requires written consent under Treas. Reg. § 301.7216-3(a) before disclosing to the lending institution.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; the client asked for the loan
B) The taxpayer’s written consent
C) A Form 2848 naming the lender
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a request is not written consent. C is wrong: the lender is not representing the client, and consent is what the rules require.
notes.source: Publication 1345 (Rev. 12-2025), Handbook for Authorized IRS e-file Providers of Individual Income Tax Returns, “Refund-related financial products”, p. 36
notes.evidence: Secure the taxpayer’s written consent as specified in Treas. Reg. § 301.7216-3(a) to disclose tax infor-

notes.front: According to the IRS Manual, what must examiners be able to do with the law in a case?
notes.back: Identify the applicable law, interpret its meaning in light of congressional intent, and apply it fairly to the facts.
notes.explanation: A representative building a case needs the same three steps to match or challenge the examiner.
notes.source: IRM 4.10.7, Issue Resolution, “IRM 4.10.7.1, Program Scope and Objectives”
notes.evidence: It is imperative that examiners can identify the applicable law, correctly interpret its meaning in light of congressional intent

notes.front: Whose facts must an examiner gather when determining the tax liability?
notes.back: All available facts, including those supporting the taxpayer’s position, so both sides of each issue.
notes.explanation: The determination must rest on all the facts, not only those favouring the IRS.
notes.source: IRM 4.10.7, Issue Resolution, “IRM 4.10.7.3, Evaluating Evidence”
notes.evidence: examiners should determine all the facts supporting both sides of an issue

notes.front: An examiner proposes disallowing a client’s travel costs and has not looked at the diary and receipts the client offered. What can the enrolled agent point out?
notes.back: The examiner must consider all facts, including those supporting the taxpayer, before reaching a determination.
notes.explanation: The Manual tells examiners to determine the facts supporting both sides of an issue.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; the examiner decides what to review
B) The determination must weigh the taxpayer’s evidence too
C) Only a court can consider the diary
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the Manual requires all available facts to be considered. C is wrong: the evidence belongs in the examination itself.
notes.source: IRM 4.10.7, Issue Resolution, “IRM 4.10.7.3, Evaluating Evidence”
notes.evidence: This determination must be made on the basis of all available facts, including facts supporting the taxpayer’s position.

notes.front: In IRS fraud development, what substantiates fraud: badges of fraud or affirmative acts?
notes.back: Affirmative acts (firm indications) of fraud; first indicators, or badges, only point to it.
notes.explanation: Affirmative acts are actions by the taxpayer, preparer or promoter to deceive or defraud.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “IRM 25.1.2.1.1, Background”
notes.evidence: Fraud is substantiated by establishing affirmative acts (firm indications) of fraud.

notes.front: Does one indicator of fraud show that fraud is present?
notes.back: No. No one indicator is determinative.
notes.explanation: An indicator is a sign or symptom that actions may have been taken to deceive or conceal.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “IRM 25.1.2.11, indicators and affirmative acts”
notes.evidence: No one indicator of fraud is determinative that fraud is indeed present.

notes.front: Once affirmative acts of fraud are established, what may the fraud enforcement advisor recommend?
notes.back: A referral to Criminal Investigation, if the criminal criteria are met.
notes.explanation: The examiner or revenue officer first suspends the case activity and notifies the group manager and the advisor.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “IRM 25.1.2.2, Fraud Development Procedures”
notes.evidence: The FEA recommends a referral to Criminal Investigation (CI), if criminal criteria is met

notes.front: Soon after an examination starts, a client tells his enrolled agent he shredded last year’s ledgers and never told his preparer about a second bank account. How should the agent classify these facts?
notes.back: As indicators of fraud that could raise potential criminal aspects.
notes.explanation: The Manual lists destroying records just after an examination starts and not disclosing facts to the preparer as indicators of fraud.
notes.choices:
A) Ordinary record-keeping lapses
B) Indicators of fraud with possible criminal aspects
C) Proof of fraud on their own
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: both acts are on the Manual’s list of fraud indicators. C is wrong: no single indicator is determinative; fraud rests on affirmative acts.
notes.source: IRM 25.1.2, Recognizing and Developing Fraud, “IRM 25.1.2.3, Indicators of Fraud”
notes.evidence: Destruction of books and records, especially if just after examination was started.

notes.front: A practitioner is asked to represent both former business partners in a dispute with the IRS where each blames the other for the unreported income. What does Circular 230 say?
notes.back: This is a conflict of interest: representing one would be directly adverse to the other.
notes.explanation: Section 10.29 defines a conflict as including representation of one client directly adverse to another.
notes.choices:
A) No issue if the fee is shared
B) A conflict of interest exists
C) Conflicts apply only to attorneys
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: fees have no bearing on the definition. C is wrong: section 10.29 applies to every practitioner.
notes.source: 31 CFR Part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), 7-1-25 edition, “§ 10.29 Conflicting interests”, p. 19
notes.evidence: will be directly adverse to another

notes.front: Which practitioners are eligible to use the Transcript Delivery System?
notes.back: Circular 230 practitioners, among others, with a properly executed Form 2848 or Form 8821 on file.
notes.explanation: The authorisation on file is what gives access to a particular client’s records.
notes.source: Transcript Delivery System (TDS), IRS.gov, “Transcript Delivery System (TDS)”
notes.evidence: A properly executed Form 2848, Power of Attorney or Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization must be on file.

notes.front: What are two kinds of record an eligible practitioner can get through the Transcript Delivery System?
notes.back: Any two of: account transcripts; wage and income documents; tax return transcripts; record of account; verification of non-filing letters.
notes.explanation: The service lists five record types for practitioners.
notes.source: Transcript Delivery System (TDS), IRS.gov, “Transcript Delivery System (TDS)”
notes.evidence: Verification of non-filing letters

notes.front: An enrolled agent wants a new client’s wage and income documents online before the client’s authorisation reaches the IRS. Can she use the Transcript Delivery System now?
notes.back: No. A properly executed Form 2848 or 8821 must be on file first.
notes.explanation: The service requires the authorisation to be on file before records are released.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, as an enrolled agent
B) No, the authorisation must be on file first
C) Yes, with the client’s oral consent
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: eligibility as a practitioner is not enough, and oral consent is not a properly executed Form 2848 or 8821 on file.
notes.source: Transcript Delivery System (TDS), IRS.gov, “Transcript Delivery System (TDS)”
notes.evidence: A properly executed Form 2848, Power of Attorney or Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization must be on file.

notes.front: A self-employed plumber asks the IRS to delay collection, and the IRS wants a detailed financial statement from him. Which collection information statement fits him?
notes.back: Form 433-A, the statement for wage earners and self-employed individuals.
notes.explanation: The IRS names each statement by who files it, and a self-employed individual falls under Form 433-A’s title rather than the business form, 433-B.
notes.choices:
A) Form 433-A
B) Form 433-B
C) Form 8821
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: Form 433-B is for businesses. C is wrong: Form 8821 authorises disclosure and is not a financial statement.
notes.source: Temporarily delay the collection process, IRS.gov, “Required information”
notes.evidence: Form 433-A, Collection Information Statement for Wage Earners and Self-Employed Individuals

notes.front: Besides the collection information statement itself, what are two things the IRS may ask documents to verify?
notes.back: Any two of: income; monthly living expenses; bank accounts; property and other assets.
notes.explanation: The IRS lists these as the items documents may be asked to verify before approving a delay.
notes.source: Temporarily delay the collection process, IRS.gov, “Required information”
notes.evidence: We may also ask for documents  to verify your:

notes.front: If a proposed payment plan will not pay the balance in full by the collection statute expiration date, what is required?
notes.back: A collection information statement and supporting financial information.
notes.explanation: Such agreements are also reviewed every two years for changes in the taxpayer’s finances.
notes.source: Publication 594 (Rev. 1-2026), The IRS Collection Process, “Partial payment plan”, p. 3
notes.evidence: will be required to complete a collection information statement and

notes.front: When may a taxpayer ask the IRS to delay collection?
notes.back: When paying any of the amount due would prevent them from meeting basic living expenses.
notes.explanation: The IRS may ask for a collection information statement and proof of finances first.
notes.source: Publication 594 (Rev. 1-2026), The IRS Collection Process, “If you are unable to pay at this time”, p. 3
notes.evidence: prevent you from meeting basic living expenses, you can request that

notes.front: A client’s only income covers rent, food and medicine, with nothing left over, and she owes $9,000. Which approach fits her ability to pay?
notes.back: Ask the IRS to delay collection because payment would prevent her meeting basic living expenses.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 offers the delay where paying any amount would stop the taxpayer meeting basic living expenses.
notes.choices:
A) A monthly payment plan
B) A delay in collection
C) Pay in full with a credit card
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: she has no money left after basic living expenses, so she cannot make payments.
notes.source: Publication 594 (Rev. 1-2026), The IRS Collection Process, “If you are unable to pay at this time”, p. 3
notes.evidence: prevent you from meeting basic living expenses, you can request that

notes.front: What is the necessary expense test?
notes.back: Expenses needed to provide for the taxpayer’s and family’s health and welfare and/or the production of income.
notes.explanation: Allowable living expenses are those that meet this test.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “General”
notes.evidence: necessary to provide for a taxpayer's (and his or her family's) health and welfare and/or production of income

notes.front: How much do the national standards for food, clothing and other items allow?
notes.back: The total national standard for the family size, monthly, without questioning what was actually spent.
notes.explanation: These amounts apply nationwide.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “General”
notes.evidence: Taxpayers are allowed the total National Standards amount monthly for their family size, without questioning the amount actually spent.

notes.front: Under the local standards for housing, utilities and transportation, what amount is usually allowed?
notes.back: The amount actually spent or the local standard, whichever is less.
notes.explanation: Local standards are maximum allowances that vary by location.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “General”
notes.evidence: In most cases, the taxpayer is allowed the amount actually spent, or the local standard, whichever is less.

notes.front: How many people does the IRS generally allow for necessary living expenses?
notes.back: Generally the same as the dependents allowed on the taxpayer’s most recent income tax return.
notes.explanation: The household size drives the national and local standard amounts.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “General”
notes.evidence: Generally, the total number of persons allowed for necessary living expenses should be the same as those allowed as dependents on the taxpayer's most recent year income tax return.

notes.front: Can the IRS allow actual expenses above the standards?
notes.back: Yes, if the standards are inadequate for basic living expenses and the taxpayer provides documentation showing it.
notes.explanation: The burden is on the taxpayer to document that the standards leave them without adequate means.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “General”
notes.evidence: However, taxpayers must provide documentation that supports a determination that using national and local expense standards leaves them an inadequate means of providing for basic living expenses.

notes.front: What does the six-year rule allow?
notes.back: Living expenses above the standards, and other expenses, as long as the full liability can be paid in six years.
notes.explanation: It is for taxpayers who cannot pay in full and do not qualify for a simple payment plan.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “Six-year rule for repayment of tax liability”
notes.evidence: as long as the tax liability, including penalty and interest, can be full paid in six years

notes.front: The Collection Financial Standards on IRS.gov, as read in September 2026, apply to financial analysis on or after {{c1::29 June 2026}}.
notes.explanation: The standards are revised from time to time. The exam tests material as amended through 31 December 2025, so its questions may use the earlier standards.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “Recent revisions”
notes.evidence: The revised standards are effective for financial analysis conducted on or after June 29, 2026.

notes.front: A client pays $2,400 a month rent; the local housing and utilities standard for her county and household is $1,900. How much will the IRS usually allow?
notes.back: $1,900, the lesser of the amount spent and the local standard.
notes.explanation: Local standards are applied as the amount actually spent or the standard, whichever is less.
notes.choices:
A) $2,400
B) $1,900
C) The national standard instead
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the actual cost exceeds the standard, so the standard caps it. C is wrong: housing falls under the local standards.
notes.source: Collection Financial Standards, IRS.gov (standards effective June 29, 2026), “General”
notes.evidence: In most cases, the taxpayer is allowed the amount actually spent, or the local standard, whichever is less.

notes.front: Which taxes does the automatic stay stop the IRS from collecting?
notes.back: Taxes that arose before the bankruptcy filing.
notes.explanation: Actions such as serving lien or levy notices for pre-bankruptcy debts are barred.
notes.source: Publication 908 (12-2025), Bankruptcy Tax Guide, “The automatic stay”, p. 15
notes.evidence: arose before the bankruptcy filing. IRS collection actions

notes.front: Does the automatic stay stop the IRS auditing a debtor to determine the tax owed?
notes.back: No. An audit and a demand for tax returns, among other steps, are not prohibited.
notes.explanation: The stay stops collection, not the IRS determining the amount owed.
notes.source: Publication 908 (12-2025), Bankruptcy Tax Guide, “Tax audits and the automatic stay”, p. 15
notes.evidence: 1. An audit to determine tax liability,

notes.front: What does a bankruptcy discharge order do?
notes.back: Discharges the debtor from personal liability for certain debts, including taxes, and bars creditors acting on pre-petition liabilities.
notes.explanation: Secured creditors with valid pre-bankruptcy liens may still enforce them.
notes.source: Publication 908 (12-2025), Bankruptcy Tax Guide, “Discharge of Unpaid Tax”, p. 18
notes.evidence: debtor from personal liability for certain debts, including

notes.front: For an individual in a chapter 7 case, what are two kinds of tax debt that are not discharged?
notes.back: Any two of: taxes with no return filed; late returns filed within 2 years before the petition; fraudulent returns; willful evasion, among others.
notes.explanation: Publication 908 lists these alongside taxes entitled to eighth priority.
notes.source: Publication 908 (12-2025), Bankruptcy Tax Guide, “Discharge of Unpaid Tax: Chapter 7 cases”, p. 18
notes.evidence: • Taxes for which no return was filed.

notes.front: In a chapter 7 case filed in 2026, an individual owes income tax for a year for which he never filed a return. Is that tax discharged?
notes.back: No. Taxes for which no return was filed are not subject to discharge.
notes.explanation: Publication 908 lists unfiled-return taxes among the chapter 7 exceptions.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, chapter 7 discharges all taxes
B) No, unfiled-return taxes are excepted
C) Yes, once the automatic stay ends
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: many tax debts are excepted from discharge. C is wrong: the end of the stay does not discharge a tax.
notes.source: Publication 908 (12-2025), Bankruptcy Tax Guide, “Discharge of Unpaid Tax: Chapter 7 cases”, p. 18
notes.evidence: • Taxes for which no return was filed.

notes.front: A client files for bankruptcy during an IRS examination and says the IRS must now stop the audit. Is he right?
notes.back: No. The automatic stay does not prohibit an audit to determine tax liability.
notes.explanation: The stay suspends collection, while the IRS may still determine the tax.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the stay halts all IRS activity
B) No, the audit may continue
C) Yes, unless the IRS gets court permission
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: an audit to determine liability is expressly not prohibited by the stay.
notes.source: Publication 908 (12-2025), Bankruptcy Tax Guide, “Tax audits and the automatic stay”, p. 15
